chapter_title: Chương 132: Trần Quý Lương khuyên các cụ đọc sách nhiều hơn

segments.title: Chương 132: Trần Quý Lương khuyên các cụ đọc sách nhiều hơn
segments.content:
The guest interview segment in the latter half of "Eastern Night Tales" had always been amicable, focusing mainly on casual chats.

They had never encountered someone like Chen Guiliang before!

But the host, Liu Yiwei, was getting excited. Finally, he didn't have to just sing their praises. Every episode involved him and the guests exchanging flattery. He had to coddle those with slightly higher status, and the topics were all trivial matters.

Yet, the audience loved watching it, being very interested in the daily trifles of celebrities.

The director's voice came through his earpiece: "Chat with him. We'll cut any remarks that are too out of line in post-production."

How would they cut it? The part railing against "Wolf Totem" could be kept, but anything involving other people or organizations had to be cut. For example, when Chen Guiliang mentioned the Academy of Social Sciences just now, that half-sentence would definitely not be broadcast.

Liu Yiwei very cunningly distanced himself: "I haven't read this book yet. What parts do you feel are inappropriate?"

Chen Guiliang said: "The author relied entirely on his imagination when writing the book. He claims that agricultural civilization destroyed the grasslands, while the pastoral methods of grassland civilization were naturally sustainable. The author probably hasn't studied historical geography. From the Hetao region and Monan all the way to the grasslands of the upper Liao River, the speed of desertification during the Yuan Dynasty was extremely fast."

"Why did that happen?" Liu Yiwei was only responsible for guiding the conversation.

Chen Guiliang said: "The official pastures of the Yuan Dynasty were enormous, and the number of horses, cattle, and sheep far exceeded the grasslands' carrying capacity. The nobles also enclosed the best pastures, forcing ordinary herders to gather on the marginal grasslands. These marginal grasslands were already ecologically fragile; how could they withstand overgrazing by so many herders? There was also the construction of cities, frequent military campaigns, and military-agricultural colonies in the grassland regions. This led to a severe decline in animal husbandry in the late Yuan Dynasty. The horse production of official pastures dropped by 50%, and for private herders, not even one-tenth of their livestock remained."

"The author is substituting concepts. He's applying the production methods of the people in New China to all nomadic civilizations throughout history. Little does he know that the herders of New China are a special case. When he discusses agricultural civilization, he looks at it from the perspective of its entire several-thousand-year history, and only at its shortcomings. But when discussing nomadic civilization, he likes to 'see the big picture in the small details,' specifically picking out its merits to talk about."

"A classic double standard!"

Liu Yiwei said: "A double standard?"

"Yes, a double standard," Chen Guiliang said. "Certain people are particularly fond of double standards, especially when talking about the differences between China and foreign countries. The same thing, done by a Chinese person and a foreigner, is seen differently."

Liu Yiwei smiled, "Could you elaborate?"

Chen Guiliang said: "I was once obsessed with magazines like 'Reader,' but later I discovered that their articles were self-contradictory. They'd say Chinese people spoil their children, while foreigners focus on adversity training. Then they'd say Chinese people suppress their children, while foreigners focus on encouragement. I just want to know, how exactly should Chinese people raise their children?"

"Encourage when it's time to encourage, suppress when it's time to suppress," Liu Yiwei laughed even more heartily.

Chen Guiliang continued: "Then what about this line of reasoning? Chinese parents are busy with work and don't spend much time with their children. Foreign parents give their children enough companionship and care, so their children grow up to be cheerful and confident. Then they also say Chinese parents are overly concerned with their children, while foreign parents give their children enough personal space, so foreign children grow up to be cheerful and confident."

Liu Yiwei said: "It's also possible that Chinese parents neither provide companionship nor, at certain times, are overly concerned."

Chen Guiliang said: "The people who write these kinds of articles only see two countries in their eyes. One is China, and the other is 'foreign countries.' There are over 200 countries and regions in the world, each with different languages, customs, beliefs, and political systems, yet they can always find a commonality where they are superior to China. It's actually the same trick as in 'Wolf Totem.'"

"How so?" Liu Yiwei continued to guide him.

Chen Guiliang said: "They extract some commonalities of all humankind. They describe the weaknesses of human nature as the inherent flaws of the Chinese nation. They describe the virtues of human nature as the fine qualities of foreigners. 'Wolf Totem' is more or less the same, only talking about the weaknesses of agricultural civilization and the virtues of grassland civilization."

Liu Yiwei really couldn't hold back anymore and wanted to express his own opinion: "Now that you put it that way, it reminds me of 'The Ugly Chinaman.'"

Chen Guiliang laughed loudly, "That book is a pile of shit. I remember Bo Yang said in the book that the Chinese are the most arrogant people in the world, because they've seen little and are too narrow-minded, so the heavens and earth can't contain them after the slightest achievement. He also said that Chinese people never have self-esteem, so they have no concept of equality. Do you have self-esteem?"

Liu Yiwei scratched his head, "I think so."

"Bo Yang also said that in Chinese democracy, it's 'you for the people, I as the master,'" Chen Guiliang said with a smile. "He understands neither Chinese history nor foreign history. Many people now praise Washington, saying he retired after his success, a paragon of democracy. Actually, he's much like Bo Yang."

Liu Yiwei said: "Isn't Washington a paragon of democracy?"

"Let's not even mention all the black slaves he owned," Chen Guiliang said. "You think Washington didn't want to be emperor? He didn't have the foundation to rule. Right after America gained its independence, none of the founding fathers who participated in the Revolutionary War were willing to pay taxes to the American government. The reason they fought for independence was so they wouldn't have to pay taxes to Britain. Now that they were independent, if they still had to pay taxes, wouldn't they have fought for nothing?"

"Hahaha, that's true," Liu Yiwei chuckled.

Chen Guiliang said: "The newly established United States couldn't even collect taxes and was saddled with a mountain of war debt. The president had to worry every day about how to pay his subordinates. In his attempt to levy taxes, he directly triggered the Whiskey Rebellion. And because he compromised with Britain, he was branded a traitor. Franklin even cursed him to die soon. Would you want to be a president like that?"

"I wouldn't," Liu Yiwei shook his head.

Chen Guiliang said: "Washington didn't want to either. Even if he did, he couldn't have continued. He was basically public enemy number one at the time. So he went home and continued to be a plantation owner."

Liu Yiwei said: "I really didn't know about all this."

"Those founding heroes of America have all been glorified, and intellectuals like Bo Yang actually fell for it," Chen Guiliang said.

Liu Yiwei said: "Everyone says so, it's hard not to believe it."

"Bo Yang also said that after Confucius, China never produced another true thinker, because all the intellectuals were busy annotating the works of Confucius and his disciples," Chen Guiliang said. "If Mr. Bo Yang can see this program, I recommend he read 'A History of Chinese Thought.' One is never too old to learn. Reading more books will do him good."

The director's voice came through Chen Guiliang's earpiece: "Guide the topic, talk about something more interesting."

Chen Guiliang said: "It seems he has read very few academic works and looks down on today's popular culture. Take the recently popular 'Mice Love Rice,' for instance. No one praises it; it's just called vulgar."

"Not necessarily. I quite like 'Mice Love Rice'," Liu Yiwei said.

Chen Guiliang asked: "Do you find it too much like a jingle?"

"I distinguish between true vulgarity and fake elegance," Liu Yiwei said. "I dislike those who are clearly vulgar but insist on pretending to be cultured and putting on airs. 'Mice Love Rice' is straightforward enough in its vulgarity. That kind of music is actually quite good."

Chen Guiliang said: "So you think 'Mice Love Rice' became popular because it was vulgar and straightforward enough?"

"That's just one aspect; it's also related to the development of the internet," Liu Yiwei said. "Before, it was the Web 1.0 era, where websites unilaterally pushed information to netizens. Now it's already the Web 2.0 era, with more emphasis on interaction between netizens and websites, and between netizens themselves. Netizens are no longer passive recipients of internet content; they can generate content themselves. And with more people comes more power. The amount of content generated by netizens has increased exponentially compared to before."

Chen Guiliang said: "So 'Mice Love Rice' is content generated by netizens. Its popularity is the result of interaction among netizens?"

"Yes, and this trend will only intensify," Liu Yiwei said.

Chen Guiliang said: "Some people also worry that online songs will impact the traditional record industry."

Qi Bodong said: "It's not the first time the record industry has been impacted. Before the 80s, the record industry was monopolized by a few large companies because recording costs were very high back then. Later, the emergence of various electronic devices broke the monopoly of the big companies, and many independent record labels appeared. Today's online songs are now impacting the distribution channels of the record industry. It's an inevitable result of the development of productive forces."

"What do you think is the future of the record industry?" Qi Bodong asked.

Liu Yiwei said: "It'll be crushed sooner or later."

Chen Guiliang had grown accustomed to Liu Yiwei's various "outrageous statements": "Is your Xiaonei Network's campus belle election also an interaction among netizens?"

"Xiaonei Network is different. It's based on real names, moving real-life social networking online. The cross-interaction between offline and online can produce a wonderful chemical reaction," Liu Yiwei said.

Chen Guiliang said: "I heard the campus belle election on Xiaonei Network at Peking University led to many amusing incidents."

Liu Yiwei said: "It did. At first, there was no suspense. The Olympic champion Liu Xuan is also a student at Peking University, and her vote count was landslides ahead of second place."

"Have you had any real-life interaction with Liu Xuan?"

"Not even online. She's very low-key at Peking University."

"I heard many Peking University students hoped to vote for Sister Furong?"

"They were just spoofing."

"Spoofing is also a recent buzzword. I've seen the photoshopped spoof series online. They can make you laugh until your stomach hurts."

"I started that. The others are just following the trend."

"You?"

"That's right. In the very beginning, to promote Three Kingdoms Kill, I had no money for advertising, so I came up with all sorts of methods. The Three Kingdoms Kill Tieba is now the largest spoofing base on the Chinese internet."

"It seems you're a pioneer of the internet. That's why you look down on old-school figures, like the authors of 'The Ugly Chinaman' and 'Wolf Totem'."

"I am very respectful of the older generation. Of course, that's on the premise that their scholarship and character are worthy of my respect."

For a talk show segment scheduled for 15 minutes, Liu Yiwei and Qi Bodong talked for 40 minutes.

The previously recorded CCTV "Dialogue" episode should be about to air by now.

It would probably stir up heated debate again, as "quality-oriented education" had been a hot topic in recent years, to the extent that it could be described as a matter of national concern. Every time there was a relevant remark, anything slightly unconventional could set off a public opinion storm.

Liu Yiwei specialized in latching onto hot topics.

Quality-oriented education was one, and so was "Wolf Totem."

Who told "Wolf Totem" to sell like crazy? If he didn't latch onto it, who would he latch onto? Liu Yiwei's comment suggesting Bo Yang should read more books would also probably ignite a flame war, as Bo Yang was also very popular in those years.
